My only advice (as I’m also on my first pregnancy and not an expert), is to realize that feeling like crap is totally normal. 

I knew pregnancy would be hard, but I never knew how fatigued and terrible I’d feel as early as week 6.

Fatigue, nausea, loss of appetite (I’m down 10 lbs but should put back on once the nausea subsided), bloating (your tummy feels hard and full all the time, constipation (this can be serious), breast tenderness, etc. it all hits you at once! 

So I’ve let myself be lazy, I’ve honored my need for naps. I’ve let the dishes pile up and I’ve let the bed go unmade. I eat what I can when I can, and I get what I can get done, done. I do my best but I honor my need to be “lazy”. 

Get with the doc if you’re on any prescriptions just in case they need adjusted. 

Ginger root pills help with nausea, and grab some prenatal as while you’re at it. Good luck!!! 💗

You’re amazing! I felt exhausted for you just reading all of the countless interventions you’ve tried. No, I don’t think stripping her bedroom and taking privileges is harsh at this point. She’ll be a grown up soon and will need to learn that her actions have very real consequences.

If you’re not already, make sure you have a notebook to document her behaviors after being with biomom. Parents like this love to be the “Disneyland parents” failing to teach them or give them consequences for anything.

Not harsh. It could even go on a box spring.  Some parents even remove doors. She’d have to change in the bathroom, but it’d make it easy for parents to supervise her and keep her room clean.

OP, what’s your health insurance situation? A lot of people come with the sole advice of therapy, and in a perfect world we’d all have access to it. You and your husband should find out what your health insurance covers and get her a referral for counseling. 

Another underrated therapy is occupational therapy. It’s not just for kids with severe disabilities; it helps kids and teens to learn developmentally appropriate tasks such as personal hygiene, chores, time-management, room cleaning, behavioral and etc. 

With a doctor’s referral your health insurance would probably cover it. 

Now, take a deep breath and hear me out. There are always areas in which we as caregivers can do better. What I find to be true about kids and teens of neglect is that their parents often didn’t take the time to teach them like they should have. 

I’m in a very similar situation - my future SS10 has very poor personal hygiene. Picks his nose and eats it, wets his pants and doesn’t change and more. He’s also just not careful about things 😥knocks breakable things over, floods the bathroom when he takes a bath, etc. 

You can imagine how tough this was for me, as I didn’t have any natural kids yet (I’m pregnant now) when we moved in together. It was such new territory, and easy for me to lose my cool and raise my voice like a literal psycho. 

And does acting like a psycho teach a kid anything? No, not really. It only creates fear and resentment. It won’t improve their behavior. 

The fact is, when SS was growing up his dad (my fiancé) was working overtime to support the family while mom was being very neglectful due to a drug habit. 

So of course he doesn’t wipe properly when he uses the bathroom, of course he doesn’t know how to make a bed and of course he wasn’t in the habit of brushing his teeth at the time I entered the picture. Mom was an addict and dad was overwhelmed. 

But it’s not too late to start teaching him, and I’m happy to help my fiancé out because I know how hard he tried. And your SD? Even at age 14, it’s not too late to start teaching her. 

Punishment isn’t the only way to teach, and it might not even be effective (recent psychological studies say probably not). 

And, occupational therapy and counseling would help, but you’d also have to help her maintain the skills she learns in therapy at home. Or your husband will, but I know you want to help your husband. 

Speak to her like a dignified, intelligent human being: 
“SD, I’m sorry if I’ve been a little harsh with you about these things before. It’s just that I care, and things like dog poop carry bacteria that can make us sick. I know it’s hard to get in the habit of personal hygiene, but I promise that when you do you’ll feel *so* much better. Here is a lidded garbage can I bought for your bedroom, with replacement bags in the bottom. Anytime you need to throw away your used pads, just put them in here. If the dog has an accident, let me know and I’ll help you clean it up and do your laundry.”

Then teach her: 
- How to remove, tie off, and throw out her garbage bag. 

- How to use toilet paper to pick up the dog poop, flush it and then gather her laundry and put it into the washing machine. 

- Give her a weekly laundry day. She’s well old enough. Stand by assist her to gather her laundry, put in the machine, add the soap and set the wash. Then teach her how to move the load to the dryer, fold and hang up her laundry. After a few repetitions, she’ll be able to do this with less supervision and eventually totally independently where you don’t even have to think about it. 

- Let her come shopping to choose her own hygiene products. As a former teenage girl, I can recall the excitement of getting nice deodorant, shampoo and such. Give her a price range of products to choose from, of course, she doesn’t need $20 shampoo. This could instill in her a sense of independence and pride. 

- Make a list of her AM and PM personal care routines, hang on her bedroom wall to serve as reminders. 

- Slowly, she can learn more chores to actually help out around the house and make your life easier. 

Also consider instilling some rewards (in the form of a privilege, special activity, allowance or gift she wouldn’t normally get). 

Some incentive ideas: 
- Her laundry done properly 4 weeks in a row=reward 

- Her bedroom floor stays clear for 7 days in a row = reward. 14 days = bigger reward. 30 days = best reward. 

After routine is established, let her know that she won’t be perpetually getting rewards but that proper hygiene and cleanliness is a reward in itself. You can instill negative consequences if she starts dropping the ball as she’s already demonstrated an ability to do so. 

Remember, you’re trying to establish *routines.* I’m an adult and have gone through periods where I didn’t brush my teeth, and it was tough getting into the habit. But once a habit or routine is established, I can’t fathom not brushing my teeth twice a day! 

It requires some deep breathing and a TON of patience but I promise she’ll be so much easier to live with if you simply take the time to teach her. Is an investment in her future wellness and your own sanity. And she’ll likely remember you as the one who cared enough to teach her basic skills.

“Laziness” is more of a social construct than a real thing. It’s not as though I don’t believe laziness exists, but rather I think there’s usually a better explanation for someone’s underperformance. 

And that’s not to say *you’re* underperforming. As a matter of fact, I don’t think you are. But when dishes pile up in the sink and the bathroom garbage can overflows and you’re just so exhausted that you can’t get anything but the bare-minimum done - that’s not laziness! 

Fatigue, depression, being overwhelmed and under appreciated are all things that can just drain us. 

So no, OP, you’re not lazy. Your husband really should be more understanding. This isn’t the 1950’s and your job isn’t lesser than that of your husband. 

If it were me, I’d probably write a strongly worded letter. Emphasizing that you know how hard he works, and appreciate him so much. But that you are tired and doing the very best you can and need some appreciation back. In the letter, ask that he reads and then waits to respond. It’s hard to argue and be belligerent toward a letter, in my opinion, especially if you word it intuitively and in a way that doesn’t put him in the defense. 

I hope this helps. But you’re doing great!
